title: The first martyr, 1606
hookLine: tradition says he sat through it repeating that the Lord's will is sweet; Sikhs remember him as the first martyr

cards: A blazing day in early summer, in Punjab or in a Sikh neighborhood far from it, and you're stopped on the road. Not by the police.
By smiling people, often teenagers, holding out cups of cold, sweet water, sometimes milky and rose-pink. They hand one to every driver, every walker, every bus passenger, free, all day.
It's called a chhabeel, and it looks like pure summer kindness. It is. But it's also a remembering: those cups are poured in memory of a man who was tortured in the summer heat.

teach.b: Shaheed: a martyr. The word came into Punjabi from Arabic, where its root means a witness, someone who sees and testifies. A shaheed is a witness who gives their life rather than give up what is true.
Sikhs call Guru Arjan the first Sikh shaheed, and the story of how he died is why.
Tradition says that after days of torture in the Lahore heat, he asked to bathe in the river Ravi, which ran beside the fort. He walked into the water and was never seen again.
In 1606, on a summer day, the fifth Guru was gone. Through it all, tradition says, he kept repeating a line from one of his own hymns.
It's in the Guru Granth Sahib, and it says, roughly: whatever you do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name.
Your will is sweet. Not because pain is sweet. Pain is pain, and the torture was a crime.
Sikhs read it as trust in God so deep that even this did not make him curse anyone.
And look at what his community did with his death.
They didn't turn it into a revenge story. On his martyrdom day, Sikhs recite, remember, and set up those roadside stalls of sweet water for anyone who is thirsty.
A man who suffered in the heat, remembered with a cup of cold water held out to a stranger.

how: On the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in early summer, Sikhs gather for recitation and set up chhabeel stalls, handing out cold sweetened water to passersby.

o: a witness who gives their life for truth
a holy man who has renounced the world

games.q: your community's leader has been tortured and killed in the summer heat. how do you remember him each year?
o: with an angry march past the old fort.
with cold sweet water, free, for anyone.
games.why: Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls on his martyrdom day: a man who died in the heat, remembered by cooling strangers.

practice: Let someone come to mind who stayed kind under pressure: a nurse on a terrible shift, a parent at the end of a long day, a friend who was treated badly and didn't pass it on.
Picture their face in the hard moment, notice what their kindness cost them, and stay with them a while, with gratitude. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

orig.note: Punjabi, from Arabic: a martyr, literally one who bears witness.

carryVoice: Your line: your will is sweet. Every early summer, the cups come out again. See you tomorrow.
